name: Aristarchus (from Thessalonica)
title: Paul's coworker and fellow prisoner from Thessalonica
summary: Aristarchus from Thessalonica in Macedonia distinguished himself as one of the most steadfast companions in the apostle Paul's mission team. Through dangerous situations and long journeys, he showed remarkable loyalty: he was caught up in the riots during the uprising in Ephesus, accompanied Paul on his journey through Macedonia and Greece with the collection for the church in Jerusalem, and followed him all the way to Rome on a dramatic sea voyage. That Paul calls him his "fellow prisoner" in Colossians and his "fellow worker" in the letter to Philemon testifies to a deep fellowship marked by shared sacrifice and shared calling. Aristarchus represents the many unnamed and named believers who carried burdens together with Paul, and his example reminds us that Christian service often involves personal risk and enduring perseverance.

keyEvents.title: The Riot in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: Aristarchus was seized by the crowd during the riot led by the silversmith Demetrius in Ephesus, when the craftsmen feared that Christianity threatened their business with statues of Artemis.

keyEvents.title: Journey through Macedonia and Greece
keyEvents.description: Aristarchus was among those who accompanied Paul as he traveled through Macedonia and Greece on his way back to Jerusalem with the collection for the poor.

keyEvents.title: The Sea Voyage to Rome
keyEvents.description: Aristarchus accompanied Paul on the dangerous sea journey from Caesarea to Rome, where Paul was to be presented to the emperor as a prisoner.

keyEvents.title: Referred to as a Fellow Prisoner in Rome
keyEvents.description: Paul refers to Aristarchus as his fellow prisoner in the letter to the Colossians, showing that he shared Paul's sufferings and imprisonment in Rome.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as a Co-worker in the Letter to Philemon
keyEvents.description: In the letter to Philemon, Aristarchus is mentioned as one of Paul's co-workers sending his greetings, confirming his active role in Paul's mission team.

versions.summary: Aristarchus was a Macedonian Christian from Thessalonica who was among the apostle Paul's most faithful co-workers. He accompanied Paul on several of his missionary journeys and even shared imprisonment with him. His perseverance and loyalty in service make him an example of devoted discipleship.

versions.summary: Aristarchus was a Macedonian Christian from Thessalonica who was one of the apostle Paul's most faithful coworkers. He is mentioned in several contexts in the New Testament: he was seized during the riot in Ephesus, accompanied Paul on journeys through Macedonia and Greece, and joined him on the dangerous sea voyage to Rome. Paul refers to him as his "fellow prisoner" in Colossians and as his "fellow worker" in Philemon. His perseverance and loyalty in service – including his willingness to share Paul's sufferings and imprisonment – make him an example of devoted discipleship and sacrificial ministry in the early church.

footnotes.text: The name Aristarchus (Greek: Ἀρίσταρχος, Aristarchos) is composed of 'aristos' (best) and 'archos' (leader/ruler), meaning 'the best ruler'. This was a common Greek name in the Hellenistic world, reflecting Aristarchus's Greco-Macedonian background.

Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki) was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and an important trading city along the Via Egnatia, the major east-west road through the Roman Empire. The city's strategic location made it a natural center for the spread of Christianity in the region.

Paul uses the word 'synaichmalotos' (συναιχμάλωτος, fellow prisoner) about Aristarchus in Colossians 4:10. It is debated whether this should be understood literally—that Aristarchus was actually imprisoned with Paul—or metaphorically, as a description of his voluntary sharing of Paul's restricted circumstances. Some scholars have suggested that Paul's co-workers may have taken turns staying with him during his house arrest to assist him.

The riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41) is one of the most detailed examples in the Acts of the Apostles of the conflict between Christianity and the local religious economy. Archaeological excavations in Ephesus have uncovered the large theater where the riot took place, with seating for approximately 25,000 spectators, as well as numerous Artemis statuettes confirming the extensive trade in cult objects.

In Philemon 24, Aristarchus is referred to as Paul's 'synergos' (συνεργός, co-worker). This term Paul uses for his closest partners in evangelistic work, placing Aristarchus within an inner circle that also included Mark, Demas, and Luke.

According to ancient church traditions, Aristarchus suffered martyrdom in Rome during the persecutions of Emperor Nero. Although this cannot be confirmed from New Testament sources, he is regarded as a saint in several church traditions, and his feast day is celebrated in Eastern churches.
